rationale: This qualitative case study of two informal settlements in Xochimilco, Mexico City (using 27 semi-structured key-informant interviews and 41 resident questionnaires transcribed and coded in MAXQDA) examines how legal informality and land-tenure/land-use eligibility rules in the Conservation Zone constrain water supply solutions. Specifically, lack of formal land title and the 2017 Sustainable Water Law prohibit public piped network connections, expanded water-truck delivery, and municipal rainwater-harvesting social programmes in informal settlements (eligibility_status_documentation as the central mechanism, alongside secondary intergovernmental responsibility-shifting between the Alcaldia and SACMEX, informal trucked-water accommodations, and street-level water committees/paradas). Outcomes span effective access (chronic water scarcity, intermittent once- or twice-weekly truck delivery below WHO daily quantity thresholds, and time spent searching for and transporting water), primary piped network connection versus off-grid alternatives, and household economic expenditure on private water purchases, justifying primary_outcome_family = effective_access and assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple = multiple.
